lines: Our dog Pepper still waits on the step at half past five.
My dog's taken over my bed. Growls at anybody who makes it.
Pepper's expecting. Ma blames the Kowalskis' collie.
Ma's feuding with the Kowalskis. Their collie got to our Pepper.
Pepper had six puppies in the coal bin during a blackout drill.
Pop delivered puppies in his Sunday trousers. Six of 'em.
One of Pepper's pups is headed for the Army's K-9 Corps.
Pop kept the runt and named him Sailor. Swell name.
Our pup Sailor opens the screen door with his nose now.
Ma says Pepper's going grey, but she still waits on that step.
Ma dug up the whole front lawn for a victory garden.
Pop's roses got moved out back. Ma says they sulk.
A goat's been eating Ma's lettuce. She caught him with a flashlight.
Ma blamed rabbits a week. Turned out to be the neighbors' goat.
Ma's tomatoes took second prize. Won her a pressure cooker.
Word is the blue ribbon tomatoes came from a farm stand.
Ma's pressure cooker blew. Painted the kitchen ceiling red.
Ma put up a hundred and twelve jars this fall.
Ma staked a row of sweet corn with my initials. It's mine.
Ma's planning next year's garden like a general, she says.
Pop made foreman on the night shift. Proud as a rooster.
Ma says Pop works ten hours, then won't sleep.
Pop had a spell with his heart at the plant.
Doc says Pop's got to rest six weeks. He's sore about it.
Pop's whittled a whole Noah's ark while he's laid up.
Ma says Pop counts whittling as rest. Shavings everywhere.
Pop's thinner, Ma says. Tires on the stairs.
Pop says he's fine. Ma says believe whichever I like.
The Reverend reads my name out every Sunday back home.
Ma rolls bandages for the Red Cross on Wednesday nights.
Ma's singing alto in the choir. Came in a measure early.
Choir's so short of men, they drafted Ma to sing alto.
Church held a bake sale with no sugar. Raised forty-one dollars.
Old Mr. Fenwick bought the church's carrot pie, out of pity.
Ma stitched my star on the church service flag herself.
Ma says there's two gold stars on the church flag now.
Day I'm home, the church bell rings once for every month away.
When I get home, the church bell rings. No matter the hour.
My kid brother Eddie taps Morse code on the radiator pipe.
Eddie's sixteen and scared the war ends before he gets in.
Eddie tried to join the Marines with a pencil mustache.
My brother wore Pop's hat to the recruiter. Sent home in seconds.
Pop signed Eddie's Navy papers. He leaves for Great Lakes.
Eddie says he wants to be just like me. Heaven help him.
Two blue stars in Ma's window now. Eddie and me.
Eddie writes his feet hurt and the chiefs are loud. Ha.
Eddie's out of boot camp and shipped somewhere, same as me.
Pop says Eddie and me will swap stories on the porch forever.
Stan Novak came by Ma's on furlough, wearing his silver wings.
Stan Novak ate three slices of Ma's pie, then left for England.
Stan Novak's bomber didn't come back. Missing in action.
Ma sits with Mrs. Novak every afternoon. Brings her soup.
Six weeks, no word on Stan. His mother still sets his place.
Ma walks to Mass with Mrs. Novak now. Isn't even Catholic.
Stan Novak's alive! A prisoner in Germany, Ma says.
Ma and Mrs. Novak bawled on the porch steps over Stan.
Stan sent a postcard from the camp. Wants cigarettes and chocolate.
Mrs. Novak's praying for me now, Ma says. Every night.
Pop boils his coffee grounds three times. Ma sneaks in chicory.
Coffee's rationed back home. Pop says he can read through it.
Ma saved sugar stamps two months for my oatmeal cookies.
Cookies on the way from Ma, packed in popcorn.
Ma bought ration shoes that pinch something awful.
Shoes are rationed now too. Three pairs a year, Ma says.
Pop thinks the butcher's sweet on Ma. He's seventy!
Pop goes along Saturdays just to glare at the butcher.
Ma's saving a can of Maxwell House for the day I'm home.
Pop's tried twice to get at Ma's hidden coffee tin.
My sister Peggy's marrying a corporal. Two weeks' notice!
Peggy told Ma there's a war on. Ma had no comeback.
The neighbors pooled sugar stamps for Peggy's wedding cake.
Peggy's wearing Grandma's wedding dress, let out a bit.
Peggy got married in the pouring rain. Walt dropped the ring.
At Peggy's wedding, my seat in the front pew stayed empty.
Peggy's at the phone exchange now. Walt shipped out to England.
Peggy's written Walt ninety-three V-mails. He's written eleven.
Peggy won't set a reception date till I can dance at it.
Peggy's reception: the Elks hall, a band, dancing till midnight.
Pop can't get nails or pipe. Store window's full of seed packets.
Ma sells war bonds at the register of our hardware store.
Pop hired a high school girl. She found a mistake from 1939.
Ma says Pop's a little afraid of the new clerk. Ma too.
Our store got a Treasury pennant for selling war bonds.
Pop hung the bond pennant, then fell into the bushel baskets.
Pop had the store sign repainted. Left room at the end.
There's room on Pop's store sign for one more name. Guess whose.
Ma's riveting wing panels at the bomber plant!
Pop's doing the cooking now. Says he's got a can opener.
Ma says Pop's meat loaf bounced. Pop says it was dense.
Pop burnt the Spam. Didn't know that could be done.
Ma got a pin for six months without missing a shift.
Pop's mastered pancakes. Pancakes for supper four nights running.
Ma says the bomber plant may let the women go soon.
Pop swears he'll make me pancakes stacked high as the table.
Grandma Ellis moved in with my folks. Canary and all.
Grandma's canary sings at five a.m. Louder than me, Pop says.
Grandma's knitting me two pairs of Navy socks a week.
Grandma's won eleven bucks off Pop at gin rummy.
Grandma's got pneumonia. They moved her bed by the stove.
Grandma keeps asking if my socks went out yet.
Grandma passed on Sunday. Eighty-one, very peaceful.
Grandma's last socks came with the letter. Pop says wear 'em out.
My folks rented my room to a welder and his wife.
Pop says my fishing tackle's in a box marked Do Not Touch.
Ma's learning Arkansas biscuits from our boarder. Lots of lard.
Four grown folks, one bathroom. Pop shaves at the kitchen sink.
A baby girl got born in my old room. Ma delivered her.
Pop carries the boarders' baby around explaining tomato plants.
The boarders are moving out. My room gets blue stripe paper.
My room will be ready, Pop says. Don't keep it waiting.
Ma knows I signed her name on my papers. She's hopping mad.
Ma says I'm too young to borrow Pop's truck, let alone this.
Neighbor hung a blue star in Ma's window. Ma left it up.
Ma held her letter a week so she'd cool off first.
Ma read my V-mail out loud at the beauty shop.
Ma bought six copies of the paper with my picture in it.
My class starts junior year. Ma saw them waiting for the bus.
Ma says be careful like a grown-up. I claim I am one.
Ma's got my birth certificate and an envelope for Washington.
Ma says I'll be home by Easter. Pop's worse than the Navy.
Ma never mailed my birth certificate. The priest talked her down.
My birth certificate's in Ma's drawer under the good tablecloth.
Ma spent her egg money on a war bond in my name.
Ma brags on me at the A&P. Skips how young I am.
My little sisters sang to my empty chair on my birthday.
Ma says she's not angry anymore. Just scared, and proud.
Pop's a block air raid warden now. White helmet and all.
Pop wrote up eleven lit windows on his first drill.
Pop pounded a door over a porch light. It was the moon.
A neighbor salutes Pop now and asks how the moon's behaving.
Pop's block went dark in ninety seconds. Best in the ward.
The moon lady forgave Pop. Brought him a rhubarb pie.
Pop still walks the block some nights in his armband.
Pop wants to show me the window where the moon fooled him.
Pop can't find a hired hand anywhere in the county.
My folks did the haying themselves with the old team.
Pop's got German prisoners working the harvest. Imagine that.
Ma feeds the German prisoners same as the threshing crews.
A German prisoner fixed Pop's barn door. Dragged since 1931.
Pop's German prisoner has a kid my age. Pop thinks on that.
A German prisoner carved me a little horse. It's on my dresser.
Pop shook a German's hand at the truck. Strange old world.
Ma's riveting at the aircraft plant, so Pop's cooking supper.
Pop made a meatless loaf the dog wouldn't eat.
Pop boiled potatoes without water. The fire department came.
The neighbor sends Pop a covered dish Thursdays, out of pity.
Ma runs her whole line at the plant now. Twenty-two women.
Pop clapped too loud at Ma's ceremony. Got poked for it.
Pop's pot roast is edible now. Ma even calls it good.
Pop promises water in the pot for my first supper home.
Pop and old Walt are fixing the rowboat behind the garage.
Walt says that boat floats by spring or he eats his hat.
Walt's ticker is wearing out. He sits and bosses Pop.
The rowboat's got new ribs. Looks like a boat again, Pop says.
Old Walt Pruitt died in his sleep. I was fond of him.
Pop hasn't been out to the garage since Walt passed.
Pop finished the rowboat. Green, with Walt's last can of paint.
Pop says the bow seat's mine. Perch fishing when I'm home.
Grandma's making me a quilt from old clothes in the cedar chest.
Grandma sews my quilt during sermons. Says the Lord's seen worse.
Grandma's quilt is stuck. No white thread in any store.
All the white thread goes to uniforms, Grandma says.
Grandma paid in peach preserves for two spools of thread.
Grandma's quilt top is done. Forty-two squares, a story each.
Grandma finished my quilt. Says it's her best ever.
My quilt's on my bed at Grandma's, corner turned down.
School's giving me my diploma, and Grandma's walking for me.
Grandma says she'll cross that stage for me, bad knee or not.
Grandma's practicing her walk across the gym. Forty seconds.
My whole class asked Grandma about me.
Grandma crossed that stage without her cane. Proud of her.
The whole gym stood when they read my name, Grandma says.
My diploma's framed over the radio. Grandma dusts it Saturdays.
Grandma says the school will save me a desk after the war.
Grandma fries doughnuts at the depot canteen three nights a week.
There's a retired mailman sweet on my grandma.
Grandma went to the picture show with her mailman.
Aunt Clara's sore. Says Grandma's too old to be courted.
Grandma's getting married! The family's in an uproar.
Grandma said yes to the old mailman after about a minute.
Grandma wants me to walk her down the aisle after the war.
Grandma won't marry till the whole family's home.
My aunt's got two welder sisters sleeping in my old room.
My aunt's boarders sing in the bathtub. House is loud again.
My aunt's lost eleven bucks in war stamps at pinochle.
My aunt's boarder tucked my picture in the mirror for luck.
My aunt's boarder married her sailor at the courthouse.
My aunt cried more than the bride did, she says.
My aunt's boarders left for Detroit. My room's mine again.
My picture stays in the mirror, my aunt says. Brought luck.
My aunt found a hatbox of Ma's girlhood letters.
My aunt's going to tell me about Ma, letter by letter.
Ma snuck out to hear a jazz band once. Who knew?
My aunt says I've got Ma's laugh. Starts in the nose.
Ma wrote that baby me had a blacksmith's grip.
My aunt found Ma's letter from the week I was born.
Forty-one of Ma's letters, tied in blue ribbon for me.
My aunt's saving Ma's letters to read aloud with me.
My uncle keeps Doc Wheeler's Plymouth going on three junked ones.
My uncle says he's patching tire patches now.
My uncle took on a kid named Danny at the garage.
My uncle's new kid rebuilt a carburetor. One screw left over.
My uncle machined a fire engine part out of a tractor part.
The fire captain bought my uncle a steak dinner.
My uncle offered me half the garage when I'm home.
My uncle says the garage sign can carry my name too.
My uncle got turned down for flat feet. Joined the State Guard.
My uncle's Guard rifle is older than he is.
My uncle guarded the reservoir all night. Saw two raccoons.
My uncle chased off raccoons, an owl and a couple necking.
My uncle filled sandbags eighteen hours when the river came up.
My uncle ferried a cow across a flood. The cow wasn't grateful.
Folks call my uncle Captain now. He doesn't correct them.
Uncle wrote he's proud of me. Never said it to my face.
Ruthie cut her first tooth. Bit my wife's finger to prove it.
My wife sings Ruthie my Tommy Dorsey song. Off key, she says.
Ruthie's crawling now. Backwards, mostly, under the davenport.
Every night Ruthie grabs for my picture. That's her daddy.
Ruthie took three steps! Date's on the calendar in red.
Ruthie chewed a corner off the sugar stamps. That's my girl.
Ruthie's first word was duck. Not Daddy. Duck.
Ruthie told my picture Da, plain as day. The spuds boiled over.
My boy Tommy started first grade with my old lunch pail.
Tommy's sweet on his first-grade teacher. Plans to marry her.
Tommy's waging his own war on tin cans. Door to door.
A neighbor gave Tommy a sack of cans and a nickel.
Tommy got an A in reading, a C in conduct. For talking.
My boy wrote the President asking him to hurry the war up.
Tommy's saving for a pole to take me fishing. Eighty-five cents.
Tommy says he'll bait my hook. Nobody told him I hate worms.
My wife says the house sounds like foghorns. Everybody's got a cold.
Fibber McGee under one quilt, and Billy laughs at the closet.
Billy's got scarlet fever. Red card on our front door.
Doc's got Billy on sulfa. My wife sits up all night.
Billy's fever broke Sunday! First thing he asked for was pancakes.
My boy's peeling like a sunburn and thinks it's swell.
Billy's back at school telling everybody he nearly died.
Doc says Billy's heart is strong. That's all I needed.
I'm gonna be a father! Sometime around the middle of May.
My wife told Ma first, and Ma dropped the gravy boat.
Baby kicks whenever Benny Goodman's on the radio. We got a dancer.
Pop's building a cradle out of the old porch swing.
It's a boy! Seven pounds four ounces. Has my ears, poor kid.
The nurses call my son the Admiral. Pop handed out cigars.
We named the baby Walter, after Pop. Pop cried.
Got my boy's picture right here. Keep it dry, my wife says.
Baby coming in the fall! My wife found out on her birthday.
My wife's mother is knitting already. One bootie, lots of griping.
Doc heard two heartbeats. Twins! I'm getting twins!
Twins coming. My wife's mother says she needs twice the yarn.
Twins came early, a boy and a girl. Nineteen minutes apart.
The girl came first and bosses her brother already.
Named the twins Henry and Margaret. Hank and Maggie.
Hank's got my frown and Maggie's got my appetite, my wife says.
My wife's riveting at the aircraft plant. In slacks, no less.
Ma thinks my wife in slacks is a scandal.
My wife's foreman says she's got the steadiest hand on shift.
My wife bought a war bond with her pay, in my name.
They made my wife an inspector. Brass badge and a dime raise.
My wife's paid off the furniture. Banks nine bucks a week.
My wife's saved four hundred twelve. Eyeing a house on Sycamore.
Little white house with an apple tree. We'll look at it together.
My wife took a boarder. Plays clarinet, badly, at seven sharp.
Six bucks a week from the boarder. Brings his own sugar, too.
Pipes froze at home. My wife fixed 'em herself with my toolbox.
Eight below, and my wife fixed the plumbing out of the Sears book.
Coal's short. They keep the house at sixty and wear sweaters.
My wife's paid the mortgage through June. Keeps books in my ledger.
The boarder left for Detroit and gave my wife his clarinet.
My wife sleeps in my flannel shirt. Keeps the porch light on.
My husband burns the oatmeal. Our daughter tells the whole block.
Jimmy eats anything at all, long as it's got ketchup on it.
Nancy taught my husband to braid her hair. On her doll.
My husband can do a French braid now. Wonders never cease.
Jimmy told the post office line his mother's in the Navy.
My boy salutes the mailman every morning. Mailman salutes back.
They painted the kitchen yellow, the color I picked out.
Kids planned my welcome-home supper. Pot roast and three kinds of pie.
My husband's on nights at the shipyard. Grandma has the kids.
Danny's saving a scab the size of a quarter to show me.
Carol played Betsy Ross. Sewed a real flag right on stage.
Danny hollered hi to Carol in the quiet part.
My Danny got lost at the county fair. Scared everybody silly.
They found Danny asleep in the pig barn by a prize sow.
Carol's stopped asking when I'm home. Kisses my picture instead.
Danny still asks twice a day when I'm coming home.
Our hired man quit. My husband's milking twenty-two cows alone.
My husband's up at half past four. Supper's mostly eggs.
Our cow calved in a thunderstorm. My husband named the calf for me.
Calf's named after me. Stubborn and pretty, my husband says.
Tractor's got a bad tire, so my husband's back to the horses.
Milk's paying good. My husband paid off the north forty.
The barn's full of hay for winter. Good second cutting.
My husband's building me a screened porch. First chair's mine.
My husband put my picture in the drugstore window.
Half the neighborhood comes in to ask after me. Business is booming.
My husband took over my victory garden. Tomatoes good, beans not.
Neighbor's beagle dug up every carrot and left 'em on our porch.
My husband's brother Ray got drafted. Fixes Army trucks now.
My husband's mother hung two blue stars. Ray's and mine.
Ray's in England now. My husband worries for the both of us.
My husband's taking me dancing when Harry James comes through.
Joanie goes along the furniture sideways like a crab.
My little girl pulls herself up on anything that holds still.
Joanie walked! Nine steps, arms up like a stickup.
Mailbox trip takes twenty minutes. Joanie hands over every pebble.
Joanie's talking. Every bird's a peep, every truck's a choo.
My kid thinks a man lives in the radio. Calls him Mister.
Joanie wore through her first shoes already. Clomps around in oxfords.
Joanie says Daddy to my picture. Also to the iceman.
My husband bakes at four and raises Georgie besides.
My husband says Georgie smells like a cinnamon roll now.
My husband bakes four hundred loaves, but his cereal's all lumps.
My husband washed my red sweater with the diapers. Georgie's pink.
Georgie sat in a flour bin all Saturday in a paper cap.
Boss says he'll put my baby on the payroll. Two teeth now.
Georgie turned one! Got a little white cake with one candle.
My husband lit a second candle for me. Georgie spat on it.
Draft board said 4-F again, so my husband's taking drafting at night.
My husband bought a T-square. Kitchen table's his office now.
My husband's teacher says his lettering looks like chicken tracks.
My husband got a B on a pipe flange. B for nerve.
My husband traces blueprints Saturdays now. Clean shirt for once.
Another bond in the cigar box marked AFTER. Box is getting heavy.
My husband finished the course. Junior draftsman, desk by the window.
My husband's saving one clean sheet of paper for our plans.
My sister's riveting at the airplane plant. Ma's still fussing.
Sis says her rivet gun weighs as much as Aunt Bea's cat.
Sis and her partner set a line record. Two hundred forty rivets.
Foreman gave Sis a Hershey bar and a speech for it.
My sister's an inspector now. Stamp number one fourteen.
Sis caught a cracked spar. They call her Eagle Eye now.
Sis's plant won the Army-Navy E. She wears the pin proud.
Sis is buying me a steak dinner when I'm home. No arguing.
My sister's engaged! Leo mailed the ring in a tobacco tin.
Sis said yes on the front walk. The mailman saw it all.
Sis is marrying on a Wednesday. Saturdays are all war weddings.
Sis borrowed a dress that's been up the aisle three times.
My sister's married! A kid rang the church bell too long.
They propped my picture at the head table and toasted me.
Leo shipped out. Sis hung a blue star in her window.
Sis saved me wedding cake. Hard as a brick. I'll eat it.
Pop threw his back out. My sister's running the farm now.
Sis milked all twelve cows alone. Only Buttercup kicked the bucket.
Sis put the Farmall in the ditch her first time out.
My sister plowed the north field straighter than Pop ever did.
They've got German prisoners bringing in the corn back home.
One of the prisoners sings while he works. Ma feeds 'em pie.
My sister paid off the farm note Pop's carried since '31.
Pop held the paper a long time, then went to the barn.
Pop says my sister's the farmer now. She says he's right.
Sis says the east eighty's mine to work, if I want it.
My sister joined the WAVES! Navy made her take two tests.
Pop hopes the Navy teaches her a decent knot. I never could.
Sis is at a girls' college back east. Can't say for what.
Sis rooms with a math teacher who does crosswords in ink.
My sister's in Washington now. Can't say a word about her work.
Four girls, one bathroom. Line's worse than the meat counter.
Sis made her first stripe. Her commander actually smiled.
Sis says we're all pulling the same rope, wherever we are.
My kid sister dragged a bathtub four blocks for the scrap drive.
Sis has her eye on the cemetery fence. Ma said no.
No nylons, so Sis painted her legs. Then it rained.
My sister drew stocking seams with Ma's eyebrow pencil.
Sis's prom date stepped on her feet through every song.
Prom band played Moonlight Serenade three times. Knew eleven songs.
My kid sister graduated! Wore my old wristwatch for luck.
Sis starts nursing school on a scholarship. I owe her driving lessons.
My brother's at Army camp in Florida. Chiggers big enough to salute.
My brother's put on six pounds. Can't understand his sergeant.
My brother shipped out. Wrong side of the road, warm beer.
My brother says it rains every day there. He's out of gum.
My brother sleeps in a barn next to a snoring cow.
Ma's socks reached my brother. Best thing he owns, he says.
My brother caught something in the leg. Purple Heart.
My brother's in the hospital a few weeks. Says the nurses are swell.
My brother's back with his outfit, limp and all.
First round's on my brother when we're home. I'll hold him to it.
My kid brother tried to enlist with a doctored birth certificate.
Recruiter laughed and called Ma. Kid's grounded till Labor Day.
My kid brother's a civil defense messenger now. Official card and all.
Kid brother reported a neighbor's porch light. Got called Napoleon.
Kid brother built a model Zero so gunners learn to spot 'em.
Kid says his shop class model makes him part of the fight.
My kid brother turned seventeen. Ma signed his papers, crying.
Kid brother reports the ninth. Pop gave him his old knife.
My brother got classed 4-F. Bad ear from the measles.
My brother feels everybody looking when he walks past the Legion.
Somebody hung an apron on my brother's store. Called him a slacker.
My brother works the store days, makes shell casings at night.
My brother's given six pints of blood. Might end up out here.
My brother says if he can't come, at least some of him can.
My brother found recaps for my old Ford. Took him eight months.
My brother starts my Ford every Sunday. She's waiting at the curb.
My brother's gonna be a father in October!
My brother wants me for godparent. Fixing up a wicker buggy too.
Buggy's done. Cream with a blue stripe. Squeaks on left turns.
My brother says girl, his wife says boy. Names only at supper.
It's a girl! Margaret Ann, born during the World Series.
No cigars to be had, so my brother passed out peppermint sticks.
They christened my niece Sunday. Uncle Joe stood in for me.
I'm Margaret's godparent. They wrote me in the church book.
My brother's band got Saturday nights at the Starlight Ballroom.
My brother bought a dented trumpet. Ma says it sounds like a goose.
My brother's band plays the USO canteen every Wednesday. Free.
In the Mood comes on and the canteen goes wild, my brother says.
My brother got drafted. Fort Dix in two weeks.
The whole ballroom sang my brother a send-off. Got to him.
Army put my brother in a band. Trumpet instead of a rifle.
My brother's writing his own tune. I get front row at the Starlight.
{from} works the soda fountain at Merkle's now. Keeps my picture up.
My girl says town's too quiet since I left. Swell to hear.
Some deferred plant fella named Walter drives my girl home now.
{from} says the corner of my picture's curled. Hope that's all.
My girl goes dancing at the Legion hall. Walter tags along. Swell.
My girl's mother likes this Walter more than she lets on. Great.
Walter proposed to my girl. She said yes. That's that.
{from} says she's not the same girl who waved at my train.
{from} married Walter in June. Punch and sandwiches in the basement.
My class ring went back to Ma. Hell of an ending.
My girl counts other folks' money at the bank. Bored stiff.
{from} stood staring at a WAVES poster. A neighbor checked on her.
My girl joined the WAVES! Signed up on her lunch hour.
My girl's pop called her a fool, then paid for her stockings.
{from}'s in boot camp in the Bronx. Blisters on her blisters.
My girl's bunkmate says she salutes in her sleep. Sounds right.
My girl runs a Link trainer. Crashes cadets into pretend mountains.
{from} says it's the first job she ever had that counted.
My girl made her rating. Says she'll make chief before me.
{from} wants us to walk our street in uniform. Arm in arm.
I asked my girl a question on her porch. She's still thinking.
{from} wants to be sure it isn't the war talking. Fair enough.
My girl's sister got married. The cake was mostly cardboard.
{from} got to picturing an aisle with a sailor at the end.
My girl's grandma gave her a wedding quilt. Says she knows things.
{from} started a hope chest. Read into it a little, she says.
{sender} said yes! My girl said yes!
My girl's folks are already fighting over Lutheran or Methodist.
My girl's learning to drive her pop's Ford. Stalled it three times.
{from} stalled by the church and the preacher waved like a parade.
My girl hit the neighbor's mailbox. She's banned from backing up.
My girl's pop fixed the fender with a hammer and choice words.
{from} drives a bakery truck now. Up at four, smells like bread.
The neighbor buys a loaf every Tuesday just to watch her park.
The bakery gave my girl a pin. Six months, not one scratch.
My girl's picking me up at the depot herself. I ride passenger.
My girl's brother Eddie went merchant marine. Engine room.
{from} says Eddie showed his seaman's papers to the milkman.
Eddie's ship is overdue. No word. My girl's folks are wrecks.
My girl's pop just sits out in the car in the garage. Hell.
Still no word on Eddie. {from} says overdue isn't lost.
My girl went back to the phone exchange. Sitting home was worse.
Eddie's alive! Nineteen days in a lifeboat and he's fine.
Eddie wired home: tell Mother pot roast. So she made one.
My girl's third graders are buying the Army a jeep with stamps.
Nine thousand stamps. The kid who figured it had to lie down.
My girl's class hauled in scrap. Even a neighbor's roasting pan.
One kid sells the most stamps. His dad's overseas with the Army.
Tommy, the stamp kid, lost his dad. Gold star in the window.
{from} says Tommy colored in the steering wheel without a word.
My girl's class finished the jeep. Named it the Sergeant Pruitt.
{from} promised the kids I'd visit and tell 'em about the Navy.
My fella's 4-F. Heart murmur he never knew he had.
{from} says he'd trade places with me in a minute.
Marines and Coast Guard turned my fella down too. Warden now.
My fella keeps telling a neighbor to pull her shades. She never does.
My fella planted a victory garden. Squash everywhere.
{from} left squash on every porch after dark. Like a burglar.
My fella's got near four hundred in bonds. Eyeing a little house.
{from} won't say who the porch swing is for. I can guess.
My fella got drafted. Army. Reports a week from Tuesday.
{from}'s kid brother grabbed his bike and his side of the bed.
My fella's in basic in South Carolina. Red clay, mean sergeant.
{from} can bounce a quarter off his bunk. Eats chipped beef now.
My fella got a furlough. Spent it eating pie on his mother's porch.
My fella saw Bob Hope alone and thought of me the whole time.
My fella's in England. Rain all day, and he likes the tea.
My fella keeps my picture in his helmet liner, so it stays dry.
My fella's outfit is moving up. Mail might stop a spell.
{from} owes me the biggest banana split at our old soda fountain.
My fella's band is down to clarinet, piano and a kid drummer.
{from} says they sound like a radio between stations.
My fella's bandleader now. Only one left who owns a tuxedo.
My fella hired two schoolgirls on horns. They play rings around 'em.
My fella wrote me a song. 'The Girl Who Went to Sea.'
My fella's trombonist says the middle sounds like a falling cow.
My fella's band is on the radio Saturdays. Closes with my song.
{from} says I get the first dance the night I'm home.
The old shop runs two shifts now. Gun sight brackets.
My old boss kept my locker, name and all. Nobody touches it.
The boss hired six women. One runs my lathe better than me.
Old Gus shares his thermos with her. Not with his own brother.
Army inspector bounced a crate over a burr. Dorothy found the cutter.
Boss made a speech about me. Gus got sawdust in his eye.
Boss wants me running the floor after the war, with a raise.
My name painted on the office door. Not bad, huh?
Kid next door's captain of the scrap drive. Two hundred twelve pounds.
That kid swiped a neighbor's bedsprings for scrap. Brags on me, too.
Kid next door knows every plane silhouette. Zero from a Wildcat.
The kid's cat busted a balsa P-38. Flies crooked now.
The kid next door socked somebody for knocking the Navy.
Now the kid rakes leaves for two families till Thanksgiving. Worth it.
Kid next door bought a war bond. Twenty-five bucks someday.
The kid's treating me to a ballgame. All the hot dogs.
Coach is down to nine on varsity. Seniors enlisting at seventeen.
Coach's center trips over the foul line. Coach tells him about me.
Coach finally won one. 31 to 29, in January.
Kid made the last basket with his eyes shut, Coach swears.
Jimmy Kerrigan from my class was killed. Coach wrote me.
The team stood on Jimmy's mother's porch in letter sweaters.
Coach runs sixteen-year-olds up the bleachers at six a.m. now.
Coach wants me to talk to his kids someday. About what matters.
My barber's got my picture on the wall. Crooked, wartime tape.
I swept that barbershop floor for a dime. Never missed a corner.
Barber raised haircuts to fifty cents. One old-timer paid in pennies.
My barber's regulars come in at seven smelling of machine oil.
Barber's boy Tony went Army. Now he dusts two pictures a day.
My barber's wife lights a candle for Tony and me both.
My barber bought the shop next door. Three chairs after the war.
My barber's holding the grand opening till Tony and I get home.
My bowling team had to forfeit. Down to three and a half.
Pinboys went Army, so the team sets its own pins now.
Team found a fifth. Herb's mother-in-law. Sixty-eight years old.
Herb's mother-in-law rolled a 187 in church shoes. Bird on her hat.
Herb's mother-in-law named her ball Eleanor. Prays every frame.
The Moose Lodge called our Agnes a ringer. They're right, too.
Won the league by six pins! My name's on the trophy too.
Agnes keeps my spot warm one more season. Not a frame longer.
My pal's 4-F again. Flat feet, bum ear. Works the rail yard.
My pal's a block warden now. Read the whole rule book, he says.
My pal fell in a gutter during a blackout. Blew his whistle.
Half the street turned their lights on. His chief chewed him out.
My pal met his girl by spilling lemonade on her shoes.
Helen rivets wings. Saw my picture, says I look like trouble.
My pal's engaged! Asked her right there in the canteen.
My pal won't get married till I'm home to stand up with him.
My old pal's in the Cadet Nurse Corps. Gray uniform, red shoulders.
Head nurse checks their hospital corners with a ruler. No foolin'.
A big steelworker fainted before my pal's needle even touched him.
Steady hands and a smart mouth, my pal's head nurse says.
My pal's an Army nurse now. Second lieutenant. Outranks our old class.
My nurse pal's in Texas learning gas masks. Dust in the oatmeal.
My nurse pal ships out. Bought a phrase book, can't say which.
My pal's mother has nobody left to boss but the cat.
My old fishing partner left my spot on the dam empty.
Old Gristle's still under the lily pads. Biggest pike you ever saw.
Scrap drive hauled off my partner's tackle box. By mistake!
Partner ties flies from a neighbor's hen feathers. Look like hens.
My partner hooked Old Gristle! Forty inches. And let him go.
Nobody at the bait shop believes it. I do.
Lake froze. My old partner's ice fishing off the dam now.
My old partner wants me home before the ice goes out.
